title: Extradural and acute subdural haematoma
subtitle: The decision to operate

sources.title: Guidelines for the surgical management of traumatic brain injury (Bullock et al, Neurosurgery 2006;58(3 Suppl):S2-1 to S2-62)
Guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury, 4th edition

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)

red_flags.text: A lucid interval followed by a falling GCS: the classic extradural haematoma course.
Anisocoria, or a new fixed dilated pupil, with a haematoma on CT.
A fall of 2 or more GCS points, particularly in the motor component, since the scan.
A temporal or posterior fossa haematoma. These compress the brainstem with smaller volumes and less warning.
Anticoagulated or thrombocytopenic patient: the haematoma is likely to expand until reversed.

do_now.text: Airway, oxygenation and blood pressure first. Avoid hypoxia and hypotension, which independently worsen outcome.
Send the CT to neurosurgery and make the referral immediately; for a deteriorating patient, prepare theatre in parallel.
Reverse anticoagulation and correct coagulopathy as soon as the haematoma is seen, per local protocol.
For signs of herniation, give hyperosmolar therapy as a bridge to theatre, not a substitute.

assess.text: GCS by component and pupils, recorded with the time, before and after any sedation.
Measure the haematoma on CT: maximum thickness, midline shift at the septum pellucidum, volume, and state of the basal cisterns.
Location matters: temporal and posterior fossa lesions deserve a lower threshold for surgery.
Look for associated injury: contusions, skull fracture, cervical spine injury, and extracranial bleeding.

investigate.text: Non-contrast CT head, with bone windows for fractures crossing the middle meningeal groove or a venous sinus.
Coagulation screen, platelets, group and cross-match.
Repeat CT within a few hours for a non-operated haematoma, and at once for any deterioration.
Consider CT venography when a fracture crosses a venous sinus.

resuscitate.text: Maintain systolic blood pressure and oxygenation to BTF targets during the wait for theatre.
Head up about 30 degrees with the neck neutral, once the spine allows.
Treat seizures promptly; each one raises intracranial pressure.

definitive.text: Extradural haematoma over 30 cm3: evacuate, regardless of GCS.
Extradural haematoma under 30 cm3, under 15 mm thick, with under 5 mm shift, in a patient with GCS above 8 and no focal deficit: may be observed with serial CT in a neurosurgical centre.
Extradural haematoma in coma (GCS below 9) with anisocoria: evacuate as soon as possible.
Acute subdural haematoma thicker than 10 mm or with more than 5 mm shift: evacuate, regardless of GCS.
Smaller acute subdural in a comatose patient: evacuate if GCS falls by 2 or more, pupils become asymmetric or fixed, or ICP exceeds 20 mmHg.
Operate by craniotomy with a large enough flap; leave the bone flap out when the brain is swollen at the end of the evacuation.

escalate.text: A patient deteriorating from an extradural haematoma who cannot reach a neurosurgeon in time is the one situation where a local surgeon may need to decompress. Agree this by telephone with neurosurgery.
Transfer intubated with images available, blood pressure controlled, and the receiving theatre told the time of departure.
Every non-operated haematoma is observed in a unit that can operate on it.

notes: In an extradural, the brain underneath is often normal. Speed decides the outcome, and outcomes after prompt surgery are excellent.
In an acute subdural, the haematoma is usually a marker of the brain injury beneath it. Plan for swelling and be ready to leave the flap out.
Measurement thresholds tell you who must have surgery. They do not tell you who can safely avoid it: the clinical trend does.
